title: Summary
html:
Summary

Six leaves of the LIANA+ decision tree were run on one dataset — a human Xenium 5K TMA of IDH-mutant low-grade glioma with active high-grade transformation, 100,197 cells, 9 cell types, 13 punches (7 high-grade, 6 low-grade) — against CellChatDB v2, plus a second LR resource tier and a second local metric. Everything below is reproducible from the scripts named in each section.

BranchCallOutputCost
Bivariateli.mt.bivariate (cosine / Moran’s R)100,197 × 131 LR pairs2.0 min
Inflowli.mt.inflow100,190 × 4,608 sender×LR features1.0 + 1.8 min
NMFli.multi.nmfrank 6 (bivariate) / 7 (inflow)0.9 min each
MOFA-Flexmfl.MOFAFLEX, GP factor priorK=20 → 17 active, 6 sender views76.0 min
LRIC + cross-PCFli.mt.lric, li.mt.cross_pcfdistance-resolved g(r), 8 bins to 225 µm, 13 per-punch runs2.6 min
LR-MISTylrMistyData + LinearModel382 receptor targets × 37 ligand predictors2.9 min
default tierboth branches on LIANA’s consensus388 pairs / 9,448 features~14 min

What was found

  • Most of the signal is not cross-talk. 57.4% of total interaction strength is autocrine (source = target) — within-cell-type adhesion (NCAM1–NCAM1, CNTN2–CNTN2, CD99–CD99, JAM3–JAM3). This is a property of spatial CCC scoring, not of this tumour.
  • DLL3/JAG1→NOTCH is the dominant, most reproducible program, running cell-autonomously inside the NPC-like and OPC-like compartments. It is the only program recovered by both independent parameterisations (bivariate F6 ↔ inflow F7, r = 0.43).
  • The tumour states send; myeloid and vasculature receive. Sender:receiver ratios NPC-like 1.43, OPC-like 1.25, MES-like 1.16 versus mGAM 0.73, Lymphoid 0.35. mGAM is the most “talked-at” cell type in the tumour.
  • The strongest heterotypic edges into myeloid are APP→SORL1 and complement C3/C4A→C3AR1.
  • Every grade contrast collapses at the correct replicate unit. 0 of 7 NMF factors and 0 of 20 MOFA-Flex factors survive BH correction across the 13 punches. Cell-level p-values are ~7,700× pseudoreplicated, and the grade groups differ in composition (Glial-Neuronal is 34% of low-grade cells versus 7% of high-grade).

What is still open

  • The 13.1454 µm kernel bandwidth is derived from ALARMIST’s patch size, which this project’s own benchmark contract forbids in as many words. Unresolved, and load-bearing: it alone moves the inflow NMF rank from 11 to 7.
  • LIANA has no native multi-sample / differential mode. The punch-level test is a documented substitute, not a closure.
  • scripts/comparators/ is untracked in git, so documentation edits cannot be diffed against a baseline.

title: LIANA+: what it is, the two branches, the environment, and the input recipe
html:
What LIANA+ is, and why we ran two branches of it

LIANA+ (v1.8.1, saezlab/liana-py) is not a single cell–cell communication algorithm. It is a framework that bundles several, and its README opens with a decision tree that tells you which one to use. Reproducing that tree matters here, because our first run took the wrong path down it, and both paths are still on disk.

The authors' decision tree, reproduced

Transcribed verbatim from the mermaid block in /Users/jiayifan/tansey_lab/liana-py/README.md (lines 27–56), spatial half only:

What is your data?
 |
 +-- Spatially-resolved --> Resolution?
 |     |
 |     +-- Single-cell --> Analysis type?
 |     |     +-- Interaction scoring   --> Inflow Score                     [inflow_score.ipynb]
 |     |     +-- Interaction scoring   --> Standard LR methods              [inflow_score.ipynb]
 |     |     |                              (spatially-constrained)
 |     |     +-- Spatial co-occurrence --> LRIC                             [LRIC_tutorial.ipynb]
 |     |     +-- Unsupervised          --> Communication Programs           [inflow_mofaflex.ipynb]
 |     |                                    (Inflow + MOFA-Flex)
 |     +-- Spot-based --> Analysis type?
 |           +-- Bivariate   --> Local interactions? --> Yes: Local Bivariate Metrics   [bivariate.ipynb]
 |           |                                       --> No:  Global Bivariate Metrics  [bivariate.ipynb]
 |           +-- Unsupervised --> Multi-view Learning / MISTy                [misty.ipynb]
 |
 +-- Dissociated single-cell --> ...   (not applicable: our data is spatial)
 +-- Multi-modal             --> ...   (not applicable: Xenium here is RNA only)

Xenium is single-cell resolution. So the tree sends us to li.mt.inflow, and li.mt.bivariate — which is what we ran first, and what the project's earlier notes describe as "the LIANA run" — sits under the spot-based branch, i.e. the wrong leaf for this data.

The package encodes the same judgement in its own defaults, which is the concrete evidence that this is a real distinction and not a documentation quirk: the signature default of nz_prop is 0.05 in liana/method/sp/_bivariate/_spatial_bivariate.py:58 and 0.001 in liana/method/sp/_inflow.py:41 — a 50× lower minimum-detection threshold. The authors answered single-cell sparsity by writing a different method, not by telling users to lower a threshold on the spot-based one. An earlier binomial "spot → cell" re-derivation of nz_prop for bivariate was therefore solving a problem that should not have been posed.

We kept both branches rather than deleting the first. Two reasons, both concrete:

  • NMF is only demonstrated on the bivariate branch. li.multi.nmf appears in bivariate.ipynb and nowhere in inflow_score.ipynb. The NMF output (locations × factors, features × factors) is the only comparator output in this benchmark that has the same shape as ALARMIST's BPTF motifs, so it is the only place a structural comparison is possible at all. Dropping the bivariate branch would have meant either dropping that comparison or inventing an author-unsanctioned composition with no sanctioned counterpart.
  • The two branches differ enough that the difference is itself a measurement. On the same cells and the same LR resource, bivariate yields 131 features (LR pairs) and inflow yields 4,608 (sender cell type × LR pair; 9 senders × 633 distinct pairs, ragged — 250 to 602 pairs per sender, not a complete 633×9 grid). That is a 35.2× expansion of the feature space, driven mostly by nz_prop and by the fact that inflow carries sender identity inside the feature. Comparing the two measures how much of a "communication program" is a property of the tissue and how much is a property of the upstream filter.

Which leaves we exercised, and which we did not

Tree leafCall / scriptRan?Note
Single-cell → Interaction scoring → Inflow Score li.mt.inflow, run_inflow.py + run_inflow_downstream.py YesThe leaf the tree prescribes for this data. 1.0 min + 1.8 min downstream.
Single-cell → Interaction scoring → standard LR methods, spatially constrained li.mt.rank_aggregate(..., spatial_kwargs={'kernel':'gaussian','bandwidth':100}) Yesrun_inflow_downstream.py:392, following inflow_score.ipynb cell 83.
Single-cell → Spatial co-occurrence → LRIC li.mt.lric + li.mt.cross_pcf, run_lric.py YesRun 13 times, once per TMA punch — see the LRIC section for why.
Single-cell → Unsupervised → Inflow + MOFA-Flex run_mofaflex.py, following inflow_mofaflex.ipynb Yes76.0 min, K=20, 17 active factors.
Spot-based → Bivariate → Local and Global metrics li.mt.bivariate(local_name='cosine', global_name='morans') YesOne call returns both levels. A second arm with local_name='morans' was also run.
Spot-based → Unsupervised → MISTy run_misty.py, misty.ipynb's LR-MISTy configuration YesWhole slide, 2.9 min, at the tutorial's bandwidth of 200 — see below.
NMF on either branch li.multi.nmf, run_nmf.py Yes, but off-tree NMF is not a node of the decision tree. On bivariate it is the tutorial's own composition; on inflow it is our construction and must not be presented as the authors' workflow.
Multi-modal → Spatial (sma.ipynb) —No Requires a second modality (e.g. protein / metabolite). This Xenium run is RNA only.
Dissociated single-cell branch (liana_c2c, mofatalk, pyCrossTalkeR, Tensor-cell2cell) —No That branch consumes non-spatial, cell-type-level LR results across samples. It is a different entry point, not a downstream step of the spatial one.

So every leaf of the spatially-resolved half of the tree was exercised, plus one off-tree factorisation. What was not exercised is anything requiring a second modality or a dissociated-scRNA design.

Environment

Per the project's benchmark contract (comparator-benchmark/SKILL.md, "one conda env per method, never base, never shared"), LIANA+ lives in its own env, comp-liana, invoked by absolute interpreter path because conda activate / conda run fall through to the system Python on this machine:

ComponentVersionWhy it is there

The MOFA-Flex version gap, recorded rather than guessed

inflow_mofaflex.ipynb cell 5 states, verbatim, that the tutorial "uses the MOFA-Flex 0.2.0 API, which is not yet released on PyPI", and instructs:

pip install "mofaflex @ git+https://github.com/bioFAM/mofaflex.git@main"

PyPI's latest release is 0.1.2, which does not carry that API. We followed the notebook's own instruction and installed from git main; pip resolved the build to 0.1.0.post2.dev179+g9792b435f — a version string that looks older than PyPI's 0.1.2 but is in fact 179 commits ahead of the 0.1.0 tag on main (logs/comparators/comp-liana-install-mofaflex.log). Rather than assume the API matched, every symbol the notebook calls was checked to exist in the installed build with matching argument names before the fit was launched. It is a version gap we recorded, not one we papered over: if MOFA-Flex 0.2.0 ships and changes a default, this fit is not byte-reproducible from a released wheel.

scripts/comparators/liana/env.lock.yml was re-frozen after the torch / decoupler / mofaflex installs (167 lines) so the lock reflects the env that produced the results, not the env that produced only the bivariate and inflow runs.

Input data and the exact preprocessing recipe

One file, one section, no subsetting: data/xenium_mm_final_cell_id.h5ad — a human Xenium 5K TMA of an IDH-mutant low-grade glioma with active high-grade transformation (the repo calls the dataset "GBM").

PropertyValueConsequence for LIANA+
shape100,197 cells × 5,119 geneswhole-slide runs fit in memory; no crop needed
Xlog-normalised by an unrecorded recipemust not be used as the tutorial's starting matrix — see below
layers['counts']raw integer countsthe actual input
obsm['spatial']microns, extent 7,484 × 16,483 µmbandwidth is in coordinate units, so bandwidth is directly in µm — no pixel-pitch conversion, unlike the CosMx/MOSTA datasets in this repo
obs['cell_type']9 typesthe groupby for li.mt.inflow; 9 senders is where inflow's expansion factor comes from
obs['grade']high / lowused as the region variable, standing in for the tutorial's major_brain_region
obs['tma_id']13 punches (7 high, 6 low; ids 1–6 and 8–14, id 7 absent)the true replicate unit; used by the ≥5/13 cross-punch filter and by the per-punch LRIC runs
obs['motif'], obs['patch_id']ALARMIST outputsnever fed to any comparator. run_inflow_downstream.py hard-refuses either as --region-col. They nevertheless survive into inflow_lrdata.h5ad, so any future script that iterates obs.columns generically would silently test LIANA against ALARMIST's own labels. Drop them at load in anything new.

The preprocessing recipe, step by step, with the reason for each

This is what both branch scripts do, in order (run_liana.py:86–117, run_inflow.py:53–74). Tutorial values are in the trailing comments where they differ.

adata = sc.read_h5ad("data/xenium_mm_final_cell_id.h5ad")     # 100,197 x 5,119

# 1. start from genuine raw counts
adata.X = adata.layers["counts"].copy()      # tutorial's adata.X IS raw counts; ours is not

# 2. remove every stale derived object
adata.layers.clear()
adata.raw = None
adata.uns.pop("log1p", None)

# 3. drop the '_'-containing control probes  (21 of them, all Intergenic_Region_*)
bad = [g for g in adata.var_names.astype(str) if "_" in g]
adata = adata[:, [g for g in adata.var_names.astype(str) if "_" not in g]].copy()   # -> 5,098 genes

# 4. INFLOW BRANCH ONLY -- inflow_score.ipynb cell 13
sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_genes=10)      # 100,197 -> 100,190 cells   (run_liana.py omits this)
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=3)       #   5,098 ->   5,097 genes

# 5. the tutorial's normalisation, reproduced exactly
#    bivariate.ipynb cell 6 == inflow_score.ipynb cell 14
adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)                            # resulting X max = 8.73
  • Step 1 — X ← layers['counts']. Both tutorials begin with adata.layers['counts'] = adata.X.copy(), i.e. they assume X holds raw counts and then do their own normalisation on top of it. Our X is already log-normalised, and by a recipe that is not recorded anywhere in the repo (target sum unknown, whether it was scaled unknown). Running the tutorial recipe on it would have applied normalize_total + log1p to already-logged values — a double normalisation whose output is not a defined quantity, and which would silently change every expression proportion that nz_prop thresholds on. Starting from layers['counts'] makes our input identical in kind to the tutorial's.
  • Step 2 — layers.clear(), raw=None, uns.pop('log1p'). The first two remove matrices that no longer correspond to X after step 1, so that a stray use_raw=True anywhere downstream cannot pick up the old log-normalised values. The third is specifically about scanpy's behaviour: sc.pp.log1p checks uns['log1p'] and, finding the key left over from the file's original processing, emits "adata.X seems to be already log-transformed" and can be read as a reason to skip the step. The data at that point is raw counts, so the warning is false; popping the key removes an ambiguity, not a safeguard.
  • Step 3 — dropping the 21 underscore genes. These are the Xenium panel's Intergenic_Region_* genomic control probes, not genes: they exist to measure background and appear in no LR resource. They have to go because LIANA uses _ as its heteromeric-subunit separator — a var name containing _ is ambiguous with a complex. LIANA only warns here (stLearn hard-errors on the same names), which is worse, not better: it would have run to completion with the ambiguity in place. They are dropped before normalize_total so that the per-cell library size divides real panel counts and not panel + background; had we dropped them after, every cell's normalisation constant would have carried a background term. The stLearn run got the identical treatment, so the two comparators see the same 5,098-gene panel.
  • Step 4 — the QC filters, and the 7-cell gap. These are inflow_score.ipynb cell 13, applied as written. bivariate.ipynb contains no such cell, and run_liana.py correspondingly does not filter. That is the entire explanation for the branch-count mismatch that shows up everywhere downstream: bivariate has 100,197 cells and inflow has 100,190, because min_genes=10 removes 7 cells. Any cross-branch comparison must join on cell ID, never on row position. filter_genes(min_cells=3) removes exactly one further gene, 5,098 → 5,097.
  • Step 5 — normalize_total(target_sum=1e4) then log1p. No deviation at all: this is the tutorial recipe, same functions, same argument, same order, in both notebooks.

The spatial kernel

li.ut.spatial_neighbors(adata,
                        bandwidth=13.1454,   # bivariate.ipynb: 200 (Visium px); inflow_score.ipynb: 27 (um)
                        cutoff=0.1,          # both tutorials: 0.1 (also the signature default)
                        kernel="gaussian",   # both tutorials: gaussian
                        set_diag=True,       # bivariate.ipynb: True;  inflow_score.ipynb: not passed -> False
                        max_neighbours=100)  # signature default, unchanged

Reading the installed source (liana/utils/spatial_neighbors.py:16), the gaussian kernel is

w_ij = exp( -d_ij^2 / (2 * bandwidth^2) )

with three consequences worth stating explicitly, because they are easy to misread:

  • cutoff is a hard truncation, not a soft one. Every weight below 0.1 is set to 0, so the kernel has finite support. The support radius is bandwidth × sqrt(-2 · ln cutoff) = bandwidth × 2.14597, i.e. 28.21 µm at our bandwidth. This, not the bandwidth, is the number to compare against any physical distance.
  • max_neighbours=100 is a KNN ceiling on the graph, applied before the kernel. It is the same class of cap that binds destructively in SpatialDM. Here it is verified non-binding over all 100,197 cells: median 14 neighbours per cell, maximum 52, cap binding for 0.0000%. It was left at the default because it is already non-binding — raising it would have been a deviation with no effect. Independently re-verified with a plain sklearn 101-NN query thresholded at 28.2096 µm, which reproduces median 14 / max 52.
  • connectivity_nnz in the manifests is not a neighbour count. It reads 10,119,897 = 100,197 × 101, because LIANA builds the capped KNN and then zeroes sub-cutoff weights without eliminating them from the sparse structure. Reading it as "101 neighbours per cell" would contradict the measured maximum of 52. The real degree is (conn > 0).sum(axis=1).

set_diag=True makes each cell its own neighbour, so the median of 14 includes self. This matches bivariate.ipynb cell 21 but is an undeclared deviation on the inflow branch: inflow_score.ipynb cell 22 calls li.ut.spatial_neighbors(adata=adata, bandwidth=bandwidth, spatial_key=...) with no set_diag, and the signature default is False (spatial_neighbors.py:53). We set it to True on both branches for internal consistency. It is defensible — a cell's own ligand expression is a legitimate part of its own neighbourhood at single-cell resolution, and the inflow score is normalised by sum_j W_ij so a constant self-weight does not simply inflate everything — but it was not in the project's deviation register before this write-up, and it has not been measured. Flagging it as an open item rather than presenting it as intentional.

The bandwidth — the most consequential deviation in this comparator

Value in force: bandwidth = 13.1454 µm, cutoff 0.1, support radius 28.21 µm. It is recorded in five run_manifest.json across both tiers (cellchatdb2, cellchatdb2_inflow, cellchatdb2_morans, default, default_inflow). It was not taken from LIANA.

Derivation — equal-area correspondence to an s × s patch, s = 50 µm:

k       = sqrt(-2 * ln(cutoff)) = sqrt(-2 * ln 0.1)   = 2.14597
support = s / sqrt(pi)          = 50 / 1.77245        = 28.2095 um   # disk of the same AREA as a 50x50 um square
bandwidth = support / k         = s / 3.804           = 13.1454 um

The logic: a Gaussian kernel truncated at cutoff covers a disk; an ALARMIST patch is a square. Setting the disk's area equal to the square's fixes the radius, and the radius fixes the bandwidth. Only the geometry is borrowed — no ALARMIST output (motif, loading, LRI table, factor count) enters the derivation at any point.

This violates our own benchmark contract. .claude/skills/comparator-benchmark/SKILL.md:45–46 reads, verbatim:

Keep each method's own neighborhood/kernel definition at its default. Do NOT harmonize spatial scale across methods, and do not match it to ALARMIST's patch size.

SKILL.md:105 additionally lists "any patch/kernel/neighborhood scale parameter the tutorial does not pin down" under STOP-and-ask. We did not stop and ask. The status is OPEN, awaiting sign-off — and nothing has been changed while it is open, because every result on disk was produced at 13.1454.

Two things make this worse than a cosmetic bookkeeping issue, and both are measurements:

  1. The parameter is load-bearing. METHODS.md's bandwidth sensitivity table, fitted at k_range = range(1,41) on both rows so that bandwidth is the only difference, measures the inflow NMF rank moving 11 → 7 when the bandwidth goes 18.75 → 13.1454 µm (support 40.2 → 28.2 µm). A 30% reduction in support radius produced a 36% change in the recovered program count. So the headline "LIANA finds 7 communication programs" is partly a function of a number imported from the method LIANA is being compared against. The bivariate rank did not move (3 in both rows), because it is pinned by its 131-feature ceiling.
  2. There was no LIANA-native value to fall back on. LIANA pins no default bandwidth — the signature is bandwidth: float = None. The inflow tutorial, the branch that applies here, gives no numeric rule at all, only that the bandwidth "should reflect the typical range of molecular signaling in the tissue" traded against resolution; its own 27 µm is for MERFISH mouse brain. The bivariate tutorial's 200 is Visium pixels. So "keep the method's default" was not an available action, which is exactly why SKILL.md:105 says to stop and ask. The honest description is: a principled, transparently-derived, contract-violating judgement call, still contested.

The earlier value, 18.75 µm, and why it is void

The first pass took the bivariate tutorial's stated criterion — "a bandwidth of 150-200 (pixels) roughly includes 6 neighbours i.e. the first ring of neighbours in the hexagonal grid of 10x Visium" (bivariate.ipynb cell 20) — and re-derived the equivalent on our coordinates with li.ut.query_bandwidth, giving 18.75 µm / support 40.2 µm / median 27 neighbours.

That value is void, not merely superseded. "First ring of neighbours" is a topological property of a hexagonal lattice: on Visium, spot 1 has exactly 6 equidistant neighbours because the spots are arranged on a grid. Xenium cells are irregularly packed and have no lattice, so "the first ring" has no referent on this data, and the number it produced is not defensible on its own terms. Nothing currently on disk was produced at 18.75; its only surviving trace is the sensitivity table above, kept deliberately because it is the evidence that the bandwidth is load-bearing.

A trap in the calibration function itself

li.ut.query_bandwidth does not sweep the Gaussian σ. Reading liana/utils/query_bandwidth.py, each point is a BallTree.query_radius(r=max_distance, count_only=True) — a hard cutoff radius — and the y value is ceil(median(count)) - 1. So comparing a σ against that x-axis is a category error:

QuantityValueMedian neighbours from the calibration curve
Gaussian σ (our bandwidth)13.1454 µm2.78 — meaningless as a neighbour count
support radius = σ × 2.1459728.2095 µm13.46
realised median over the whole run—14 — matches

Our call sweeps start=5, end=120, interval_n=40 (run_liana.py:274) rather than the bivariate tutorial's start=0, end=500, interval_n=20, which is Visium-scaled and would put our entire kernel inside the first bin. The dashed guideline in cellchatdb2_inflow/plots/global/bandwidth_query.png was drawn at σ rather than at the support radius and is therefore on the wrong scale — an annotation error in one figure only; the kernel itself is correct and nothing propagates from it. (Also: the returned DataFrame's column is spelled bandwith, missing the second d — query_bandwidth.py:61. Indexing 'bandwidth' raises KeyError.)

Whole slide, not per punch — and the measurement that permits it

The tutorials operate on a single tissue section. Our slide is a TMA holding 13 punches from different regions, so running it as one object is a deviation and needs justification. We ran the bivariate and inflow branches whole-slide, all 13 punches at once, on this measurement:

QuantityValue
LIANA kernel support radius28.2 µm
measured minimum inter-punch cell–cell distance222.9 µm
margin7.9×
cross-punch cell pairs within the support radius0 (still 0 if the radius were 200 µm)

With zero cross-punch pairs the kernel graph is block-diagonal by punch, so a whole-slide fit and 13 independent fits produce the same connectivities; merging only changes what is pooled at the statistical level, not what is spatially adjacent. That distinction matters and has a measured cost: on a smoke run over punches 13+14 alone, SLC17A7_GLS^GRIA1 (glutamatergic) ranked first by Moran's R; on the full 13-punch slide it leaves the top entirely, replaced by ECM–CD44 adhesion, because Moran's R is computed over all punches jointly and a program strong in two punches is averaged against eleven where it is not. Nothing is wrong — the whole-slide run answers "what is spatially structured across this TMA overall" — but it cannot see punch-specific programs, and SpatialDM and COMMOT, both run per punch, did independently flag glutamatergic signalling as top in punch 13.

The clearance is branch-specific and does not transfer. Two other branches do not inherit it, for two different reasons:

  • LR-MISTy was run at the tutorial's bandwidth=200, cutoff=0.01 → a nominal support of 607.0 µm, well above the 222.9 µm floor, and it does produce cross-punch edges (2,520 of 10,119,190, 0.0249%, touching 232 cells). What limits the damage is the max_neighbours=100 cap, which binds for 99.7% of cells there.
  • LRIC / cross-PCF is run per punch for a completely different reason — density normalisation, not adjacency. Those functions normalise by n_points / bbox area, and the TMA's global bounding box is only 42.2% occupied. Details in the LRIC section; the point here is only that "whole slide is safe" was established for a 28.2 µm kernel and must be re-established for anything else.

The ligand–receptor resource, and a silent join trap

Two tiers were run, in the order the contract requires: default (LIANA's own consensus, 4,624 unique pairs) first, then cellchatdb2 (data/LRdatabase/CellChatDBv2.0.human.csv, the resource ALARMIST uses). They overlap by 1,663 pairs — 36.0% of consensus — so the two tiers are a real comparison. Both required LRs are present in both resources.

db = pd.read_csv("data/LRdatabase/CellChatDBv2.0.human.csv")     # 3,233 rows, 5 columns
resource = (db[["ligand", "receptor"]].astype(str)
              .drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True))         # 3,218 unique pairs, 1,383 genes

li.mt.bivariate(adata, resource=resource, resource_name=None,    # tutorial: resource_name='consensus'
                local_name="cosine", global_name="morans",
                n_perms=100, mask_negatives=False, add_categories=True,
                nz_prop=0.02, use_raw=False)

The handover is direct and lossless, which is unusual in this benchmark. li.mt.bivariate and li.mt.inflow both accept resource: pd.DataFrame with ['ligand','receptor'] columns, and LIANA represents heteromeric complexes natively by joining subunits with _ — which is exactly the encoding our CellChatDB v2 export already uses. No complex has to be split, dropped, or expanded into pseudo-pairs. Contrast stLearn, where complexes had to be converted and the conversion is itself a recorded deviation. LIANA names a pair <ligand>^<receptor>, so ^ and _ mean different things: VTN^ITGAV_ITGB5 is one ligand and a two-subunit receptor.

The join trap: this export is not join-compatible with the ALARMIST GBM run

"CellChatDB v2" is not specific enough to identify a file. The 2026-07-28 re-export reordered complex subunits and changed 1,120 of 3,218 human LR keys. The two sides of this comparison used different exports, and both are correct for their own date:

RunExportEvidence
the LIANA runs (all branches)current re-export cellchatdb2_inflow/data/global_interactions.csv: 450 × TGFBR1_TGFBR2, 0 × TGFBR2_TGFBR1; 633/633 of its distinct keys match the current file, only 496/633 match .old.csv
results/GBM/ (the ALARMIST run compared against)old CellChatDBv2.0.human.old.csv patch_lri_columns.csv: 210 × TGFBR2_TGFBR1, 0 reversed

The consequence is silent. A raw-string LR join between the two does not error; the keys simply fail to match and vanish from the intersection. Measured on the heteromeric keys, where it bites:

JoinRaw stringAfter canonicalisation
LIANA's 633 LR keys vs ALARMIST's 712495545
ALARMIST's 205 heteromeric keys94144

So 50 heteromeric keys — 24% of them — are lost to subunit order alone, with no warning. The remedy is to canonicalise both sides before joining, applying it to ligand and receptor separately and never to the whole lig^rec string:

def canon(lr):                      # 'TGFB1^TGFBR2_TGFBR1' -> 'TGFB1^TGFBR1_TGFBR2'
    l, r = lr.split('^')
    return '_'.join(sorted(l.split('_'))) + '^' + '_'.join(sorted(r.split('_')))

The two ALARMIST motif-1 arms are unaffected. GRN^SORT1 and ANXA1^FPR1 are single-subunit on both sides and byte-identical in both files, so no motif-1 conclusion depends on this. Any panel-wide overlap statistic between LIANA and ALARMIST does, and would be biased downward without the fix.

title: The two primary scoring branches: bivariate and inflow
html:
A. The bivariate branch — li.mt.bivariate

Script: scripts/comparators/liana/run_liana.py. Tutorial: liana-py/docs/notebooks/bivariate.ipynb. Installed package: liana 1.8.1, env comp-liana. Output tree: results/comparators/liana/GBM/cellchatdb2/. Wall time 2.0 min.

What the call actually computes

li.mt.bivariate returns two statistics from one pass, at two different levels, for every ligand–receptor pair that survives an expression filter:

  • Local — one score per cell per LR pair. With local_name='cosine' this is a spatially-weighted cosine similarity between the ligand vector and the receptor vector in each cell's kernel neighbourhood. It is a similarity, not an interaction probability: it is high where the neighbourhood-weighted ligand and receptor profiles point in the same direction, whether both are high or both are low. A per-cell permutation p-value accompanies it in layers['pvals'].
  • Global — one number per LR pair: global_name='morans' is the bivariate Moran's R (Lee's statistic), the two-variable extension of Moran's I. It measures whether ligand and receptor are spatially arranged together across the whole slide, not whether they are jointly abundant. A pair that is expressed everywhere and uniformly scores near zero by construction.

The global p-value is permutation-based. Reading liana/method/sp/_bivariate/_global_functions.py:68, with mask_negatives=False it is 1 - (|observed| > |permuted|).sum(axis=0) / n_perms — so at n_perms=100 the grid has 0.01 resolution and its floor is exactly 0, not 1/(n+1). This is why 106 of our 131 pairs report morans_pvals = 0.0 and 113 sit below 0.05: the statistic separates "spatially structured" from "not", it does not rank.

With add_categories=True a third matrix is written, layers['cats']. Reading _spatial_bivariate.py:267-280, each of ligand and receptor is z-scored, spatially lagged by the kernel, and signed; the two signs are then combined into 1 = high-high, -1 = low-low, 0 = mixed. The categories are what mask_negatives=True would use to zero out the low-low cells; we left masking off, so the score matrix is unmasked and the categories are carried as a separate, inspectable layer rather than folded into the scores.

Input preparation — the tutorial recipe, applied to genuine raw counts

The tutorial's first cell is adata.layers['counts'] = adata.X.copy(); sc.pp.normalize_total(target_sum=1e4); sc.pp.log1p. That presumes X holds counts. In data/xenium_mm_final_cell_id.h5ad it does not — X is already log-normalised by an unrecorded recipe and the raw counts live in layers['counts']. We therefore promote the counts layer into X first and then run the tutorial's two steps verbatim, so the normalisation applied is the tutorial's and not an unknown one composed with it.

adata.X = adata.layers["counts"].copy()      # tutorial assumes X is already counts
adata.layers.clear(); adata.raw = None
adata.uns.pop("log1p", None)                 # stale key -> spurious "already log-transformed" warning

# drop the 21 Intergenic_Region_* control probes BEFORE normalisation
adata = adata[:, [g for g in adata.var_names if "_" not in g]].copy()   # 5,119 -> 5,098 genes

adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)

The control-probe removal is forced by a naming collision, not by quality: LIANA uses _ as its heteromeric-subunit separator, so a gene literally named Intergenic_Region_1 is ambiguous with a two-subunit complex. LIANA only warns (stLearn hard-errors on the same input). The 21 probes are genomic negative controls, absent from every LR resource, so nothing testable is lost; they are dropped before normalize_total so library size reflects the real panel.

Note a branch asymmetry that matters for any cross-branch join: run_liana.py applies no cell/gene QC and therefore scores all 100,197 cells, whereas run_inflow.py follows the inflow tutorial's sc.pp.filter_cells(min_genes=10) and scores 100,190. Seven cells differ. Join the two branches on cell ID, never on row position.

The spatial graph

li.ut.spatial_neighbors(adata,
                        bandwidth=13.1454,     # tutorial: 200 (Visium pixels)
                        cutoff=0.1,            # tutorial: 0.1
                        kernel="gaussian",     # tutorial: 'gaussian'
                        set_diag=True,         # tutorial: True (package default is False)
                        max_neighbours=100)    # LIANA default, left alone

Kernel is exp(-d²/(2·bandwidth²)) with weights below cutoff zeroed, so the support radius is bandwidth × sqrt(-2·ln 0.1) = bandwidth × 2.14597 = 28.2 µm. Realised on all 100,197 cells: median 14 neighbours per cell (self included, because set_diag=True), max 52. The max_neighbours=100 ceiling was left at LIANA's default precisely because it is already non-binding (52 < 100, cap binds for 0.0000% of cells) — raising it would have been a gratuitous deviation.

The bandwidth itself is the branch's largest and most contested choice; it is derived from ALARMIST's 50 µm patch edge by an equal-area square→disk correspondence, it violates our own benchmark contract (SKILL.md:45-46), and it is load-bearing. It is documented as open deviation CD-1 and is treated in full elsewhere in this report; both branches use the identical graph.

One reading trap in the persisted diagnostics: run_manifest.json records connectivity_nnz: 10,119,897, which is exactly 100,197 × 101. That is max_neighbours + self for every cell — LIANA builds the capped KNN and then zeroes sub-cutoff weights without eliminating them from the sparse structure, so nnz counts stored entries including explicit zeros. The real degree is (conn > 0).sum(axis=1), which is what gives median 14. Do not read nnz / n_cells as a neighbour count.

The LR resource handover

li.mt.bivariate accepts resource as a plain DataFrame with ['ligand','receptor'] columns and joins heteromeric subunits with _ — which is exactly CellChatDB v2's own encoding. The handover is therefore direct and lossless, with no complex-flattening step and no ortholog translation (our data is human; the tutorial translates because its demo is mouse).

db = pd.read_csv("data/LRdatabase/CellChatDBv2.0.human.csv")
resource = db[["ligand", "receptor"]].astype(str).drop_duplicates().reset_index(drop=True)
# 3,218 unique (ligand, receptor) pairs

The script also fingerprints the resource into the manifest by testing for TGFBR1_TGFBR2 vs TGFBR2_TGFBR1. This is not decoration: the 2026-07-28 CellChatDB re-export reordered complex subunits and changed 1,120 of 3,218 LR keys, and the ALARMIST run this is compared against used the old export. Without the fingerprint a downstream string join between LIANA and ALARMIST would silently drop heteromeric keys.

Pairs are named <ligand>^<receptor> with _ inside a heteromer — e.g. VTN^ITGAV_ITGB5. ^ and _ mean different things and neither may be used as a generic split character.

The exact call

lrdata = li.mt.bivariate(adata,
                         resource=resource,        # tutorial: resource_name='consensus'
                         resource_name=None,
                         local_name="cosine",      # tutorial: 'cosine'
                         global_name="morans",     # tutorial: 'morans'
                         n_perms=100,              # tutorial: 100
                         mask_negatives=False,     # tutorial: False
                         add_categories=True,      # tutorial: True
                         nz_prop=0.02,             # tutorial: 0.2   <-- the one real deviation
                         use_raw=False,            # tutorial: False
                         verbose=True)

seed is not passed, so it takes LIANA's default 1337 (liana/_constants.py:11); the run is deterministic. Every other argument is the tutorial's value. The single deviation is nz_prop.

What comes back, and its shape

lrdata.layers['cats']100,197 × 1311 high-high / -1 low-low / 0 mixeddata/local_categories.npz
lrdata.var131 × 10ligand, receptor, ligand_means, ligand_props, receptor_means, receptor_props, morans, morans_pvals, mean, stddata/global_scores.csv
adata.obsp['spatial_connectivities']100,197² sparsethe kernel graphnot persisted (cheap to rebuild)

The four *_means / *_props columns are the per-gene expression summaries that nz_prop filters on. Keeping them makes global_scores.csv self-contained: the filter can be re-derived, and re-thresholded, without the source h5ad.

The nz_prop deviation — four numbers for one parameter

nz_prop is the minimum fraction of observations in which a ligand (and its receptor) must be non-zero for the pair to be tested at all. Four different values are in circulation for it, and they are not reconcilable:

SourceValueNote
_spatial_bivariate.py:58 signature default0.05the package default for this branch
_inflow.py:41 signature default0.00150× lower; the authors' answer to single-cell sparsity
bivariate.ipynb cell 260.2overrides the default; 20% of Visium spots
LIANA+ manuscript text10%a third value again

We used 0.02. The reasoning was a binomial spot→cell conversion of the tutorial's 0.2: a Visium spot covers roughly 15 cells, so a gene detected in 20% of spots is detected in on the order of 1.5% of cells, and 0.02 is the round number just above that. The number that forces the issue is our panel's detection rate: the median gene on this Xenium 5K panel is detected in 4.29% of cells, so the tutorial's 0.2 sits far out in the right tail of the gene distribution.

Measured consequences on this dataset (recomputed from the h5ad with LIANA's own _add_complexes_to_var and _get_props, reproducing the run's 131 exactly):

0.206the tutorial's value

The filter cascade that produces 131: 3,218 unique CellChatDB v2 pairs → 1,088 where both entities (genes or reconstructed complexes) are on the panel → minus 27 self-interactions, which li.mt.bivariate removes by default (remove_self_interactions=True, _spatial_bivariate.py:169-172) → 1,061 → 131 after nz_prop = 0.02.

The self-criticism, stated plainly, because it is the honest reading. DEVIATIONS.md judges this deviation to have been solving a problem that should not have been posed. LIANA's own README decision tree routes Spatially-resolved → single-cell resolution → interaction scoring → Inflow score, and places li.mt.bivariate under the spot-based branch. Xenium is single-cell. The package encodes the same judgement in its defaults — inflow's nz_prop is 0.001 against bivariate's 0.05. The authors addressed single-cell sparsity by writing a different method, not by asking the user to lower a threshold. Reading the decision tree first would have made the binomial conversion unnecessary. The bivariate run is nonetheless kept, for two reasons that are worth stating rather than hiding: it is the comparison point against the inflow branch, and bivariate.ipynb is the only place the authors demonstrate NMF on LIANA output.

The practical rule that follows: any statement of the form "LIANA finds N interactions" is meaningless without naming the nz_prop that produced it — on this one dataset the same call yields 6, 20, 51, 131 or 606.

What survived, and what ranked

131 pairs tested; 113 with morans_pvals < 0.05, of which 106 at exactly 0. Top of the ranking by bivariate Moran's R (read from cellchatdb2/data/global_scores.csv):

ECM–CD44 adhesion dominates the head of the list. Both ALARMIST motif-1 arms are spatially significant but mid-table — GRN^SORT1 at the 25th percentile of 131, ANXA1^FPR1 below the median. Two cautions on reading those ranks. First, a rank is a statement about the resource: on the default tier (LIANA's consensus, 388 pairs tested) GRN^SORT1 moves to 77/388 with an unchanged Moran's R of 0.035702 — the denominator changed, the score did not. Second, this is a whole-slide statistic over all 13 cores merged, and merging demonstrably dilutes core-specific signal: a smoke run on cores 13+14 alone ranked glutamatergic SLC17A7_GLS^GRIA1 first, and that pair leaves the top entirely on the full slide.

The requested-LR rule, and why it exists

Our benchmark contract (.claude/skills/comparator-benchmark/SKILL.md:56-61) requires that wherever a plot is per-LR, two sets are produced: (a) the method's own top hits by whatever statistic it ranks with, and (b) always GRN^SORT1 and ANXA1^FPR1 — the two arms of the ALARMIST motif-1 mGAM ⇄ MES-like loop — regardless of rank, in a separate output directory.

The rule exists to prevent one specific failure: if the pair we came looking for is rendered into the same directory as the method's own top hits, a later reader cannot tell whether the method chose it or we asked for it. Segregation makes that unrecoverable ambiguity impossible. The contract also requires that an absent or non-significant requested LR be reported as such — that is a result, not a gap.

Implementation in this branch: run_liana.py:42 exposes --requested-lrs GRN^SORT1,ANXA1^FPR1; lines 248-267 look each one up in the global table, record its rank in run_manifest.json["requested"], prefix the filename with that rank, and write into plots/requested/ — a directory distinct from plots/. Hence rank33_GRN-SORT1.png and rank60_ANXA1-FPR1.png, with matching _pvals, _cats and _genes panels. In the report tree these land under bivariate/03_requested/.

Compliance is uneven across the LIANA branches and we do not claim otherwise. The bivariate branch is compliant. The inflow downstream script appends the required LRs to a single top_lrs list, so in the raw results tree the requested files sit in the same 64-file interactions/ directory as the top-6 (partial compliance; the report builder re-segregates them into inflow/03_requested/). In the two NMF trees the mechanism was absent entirely until 2026-08-04 and had to be added.

B. The inflow branch — li.mt.inflow

Scripts: scripts/comparators/liana/run_inflow.py (scoring) and run_inflow_downstream.py (everything after it). Tutorial: liana-py/docs/notebooks/inflow_score.ipynb. Output tree: results/comparators/liana/GBM/cellchatdb2_inflow/. Wall time 1.0 min + 1.8 min downstream.

Why this branch is the one that applies

This is the leaf LIANA's own decision tree prescribes for our data: Spatially-resolved → resolution? → single-cell → interaction scoring → Inflow score. The bivariate branch above is the spot-based leaf. Both are kept because they answer different questions and because the NMF composition is only demonstrated on bivariate output, but where they disagree, inflow is the resolution-appropriate result.

The formula, read off the installed source

From liana/method/sp/_inflow.py (lines 218-268 of the installed 1.8.1 build):

Inflow[i, s, l, r]  =  ( sum_j  W[i,j] * L[j,l] * C[j,s]  /  sum_j W[i,j] )  *  R[i,r]
TermWhat it is
ithe receiving cell — the row of the output
jany cell in i's kernel neighbourhood (including i itself, set_diag=True)
W[i,j]the Gaussian spatial weight, obsp['spatial_connectivities']
L[j,l]log1p expression of ligand (complex) l in the neighbour j
C[j,s]a hard 0/1 indicator that neighbour j is of cell type s — pd.get_dummies(adata.obs[groupby]), one-hot, no soft probabilities
sum_j W[i,j]row normalisation, so the bracket is a weighted mean ligand level contributed by cell type s
R[i,r]log1p expression of receptor (complex) r in the receiving cell itself

Because C is inside the sum, the sender cell type is part of the feature, not part of a post-hoc grouping. A column of the output is therefore a triple (sender cell type, ligand, receptor), named <cell_type>^<ligand>^<receptor> — e.g. MES-like^ANXA1^FPR1. Read it as "cell type s is delivering ligand l into this neighbourhood, and the cell here can receive it on r". The bivariate branch has no such axis; that is a qualitative difference, not a resolution refinement.

Two structural consequences worth stating before any interpretation. First, the score is a product of a neighbourhood term and the receiver's own expression, so it is high whenever a cell expresses the receptor and sits among ligand-positive cells of type s — co-localisation alone suffices, no directional inference is performed. Second, li.mt.inflow does not remove self-interactions (unlike li.mt.bivariate, which removes 27 of them by default). Of inflow's 633 LR pairs, 27 are self-pairs, and five of the method's own top six (CNTN2^CNTN2, NCAM1^NCAM1, PECAM1^PECAM1, JAM3^JAM3, CD99^CD99) are homotypic adhesion pairs that the bivariate branch would never have tested. That difference in top-hit character is a branch artefact, not a biological disagreement.

Non-negativity — checked, not assumed

Every factor in the formula is non-negative on log1p input: W ≥ 0, L ≥ 0, C ∈ {0,1}, R ≥ 0. So the output should be NMF-admissible. Because the NMF composition downstream depends on it, the script asserts it at runtime rather than reasoning about it:

X = lrdata.X.toarray()
n_neg = int((X < 0).sum())
# measured: min value 0.0, negative entries 0 of 461,675,520  (= 100,190 cells x 4,608 features)
# manifest: "nmf_admissible": true

For contrast, the second bivariate arm at local_name='morans' is 33.4% negative and would have failed this check — which is exactly why the check exists as code and not as a comment.

The SVG gene filter — applied, and a measured no-op

The tutorial (cells 26-29) filters genes to spatially variable ones before scoring, with squidpy:

sq.gr.spatial_autocorr(adata, mode="moran", use_raw=False, show_progress_bar=False)
mi = adata.uns["moranI"]
svgs = mi.index[(mi["pval_norm_fdr_bh"] < 0.05) & (mi["I"] > 0.01)]   # tutorial's exact criterion
adata = adata[:, svgs].copy()

We applied it as written. Result: 5,097 → 5,097 genes. Nothing was removed.

That is the expected outcome for a targeted panel on structured tissue, and it should be stated as such rather than as a validation. A Xenium 5K panel is designed around cell-type marker genes; cell types are spatially organised in a tumour; therefore essentially every probe on the panel is spatially autocorrelated. The measured minimum is I = 0.159 — sixteen times the 0.01 threshold — so the I > 0.01 half of the criterion clears every gene by an order of magnitude.

The FDR half is vacuous and must not be quoted. All 5,097 pval_norm and pval_norm_fdr_bh values in data/gene_moranI.csv are exactly 0.0. At n = 100,190 the normal approximation underflows double precision; that is a floating-point artefact of sample size, not evidence about any gene. The no-op is carried entirely by the effect-size half.

The SVI interaction filter — not applied, and separately measured to be a no-op

The tutorial's cells 37-39 offer the same Moran's I filter again, this time on the interaction features after li.mt.inflow, and mark it optional. We did not apply it. Two independent reasons, in this order:

  1. Design. Applying it would pre-select the feature space for spatial structure before factorisation. The point of the NMF/MOFA-Flex comparison downstream is to ask what spatial program structure the factorisation recovers; selecting features on spatial autocorrelation first partly answers that question in the input, and would confound the comparison against ALARMIST, whose feature space is not so filtered. It is exposed as --svi-filter so the choice is reversible.
  2. Measurement. The argument above is an argument. It was therefore measured post-hoc so that the deviation is a number: applying the filter gives 4,608 → 4,608 features. Not one would have been removed.
sq.gr.spatial_autocorr(lrdata, mode="moran", use_raw=False)   # on the stored graph, no rebuild
svis = mi.index[(mi["pval_norm_fdr_bh"] <= 0.05) & (mi["I"] > 0.01)]
# 4,608 of 4,608 pass.  I: min 0.0578 (NPC-like^WNT4^FZD6_LRP6), median 0.320,
#                       max 0.9962 (Glial-Neuronal^CXCL2^CXCR1)
# 19.4 s, 1.15 GB peak RSS, two replicates agreeing to 1.1e-16

Structurally identical to the gene filter: I > 0.01 carries it (the minimum is 5.8× the threshold), and the FDR half is again vacuous — all 4,608 pval_norm and pval_norm_fdr_bh are exactly 0.0. Provenance for the measurement, including both replicates and timings, is results/comparators/liana/GBM/_benchmarks/svi_filter_measurement.json; the table is cellchatdb2_inflow/data/interaction_moranI.csv.

Note the order of events honestly: the measurement was added later, specifically so the deviation would rest on a number rather than on the design argument. The design argument remains the reason it was left off; the measurement is what makes the omission costless.

The 4,608 features — ragged, and not a product

lrdata = li.mt.inflow(adata,
                      groupby="cell_type",   # tutorial: 'cell_type'
                      resource=resource,     # tutorial: a translated mouse consensus frame
                      nz_prop=0.001,         # inflow's OWN default, passed explicitly for the record
                      use_raw=False,
                      verbose=True)
# -> 100,190 cells x 4,608 features

Decomposition of the 4,608: 9 sender cell types × 633 distinct LR pairs, which is a 4.832× expansion over bivariate's 131 unique pairs and a 35.2× expansion in feature count. It is not a complete grid. A full 9 × 633 grid would be 5,697 features; 1,089 of those do not exist. Per-sender LR-pair counts:

Never write "512 interactions × 9 senders", or any other product. The feature space is ragged and the raggedness is structural: the rarest cell type in the sample (Lymphoid) contributes the fewest features, and the most abundant tumour state (MES-like) the most, so feature count per sender is partly an abundance and expression-breadth statistic, not purely a signalling one. A factor that loads on many MES-like features is loading on a larger candidate set to begin with.

Where the raggedness comes from — corrected against the installed source. DEVIATIONS.md attributes it to nz_prop being "applied within each sender's own expression profile". Reading _inflow.py, that is not the mechanism. nz_prop is applied once, globally, to whole-sample gene detection proportions (_get_props(adata.X), no groupby), yielding m LR pairs; the full 9 × m grid is then materialised; and finally lrdata = lrdata[:, var > 0] drops every column with zero variance across cells. We re-derived m from the h5ad with LIANA's own helpers: m = 633 exactly, so 9 × 633 = 5,697 columns are built and 1,089 are dropped for being identically zero — i.e. that sender never expresses that ligand anywhere near a receptor-positive cell. The conclusion (feature count per sender is partly an abundance statistic) is unchanged and if anything more direct; only the stated mechanism was wrong.

99.4538% of the matrix is zero (run_manifest.json: pct_zeros; 461,675,520 entries). Three downstream consequences follow directly:

  • Default colour scaling on a spatial score map renders an all-black image — hence the percentile scaling below.
  • An L1 (MAE) elbow criterion on this matrix is fragile: the trivial all-zero predictor achieves MAE 0.011817 against the rank-7 NMF fit's 0.015287, i.e. the selected fit is worse than predicting zero everywhere on the metric the rank was chosen with.
  • Any per-feature statistic is dominated by which cells are non-zero at all, so co-localisation baselines (see pair_proximity below) must be read alongside the scores.

The truncation defect

Reported plainly because it is a process failure, not a parameter choice. run_inflow.py originally stopped immediately after li.mt.inflow. It wrote its matrices, created a plots/ directory, wrote nothing into it, and exited. It never executed the five downstream steps of inflow_score.ipynb. Nothing errored — the calls were simply absent, so no log, no exception and no manifest field recorded the gap. It survived until an empty plots/ directory was noticed by inspection.

The cost was not compute: compute_global_specificity on 100,190 × 4,608 at n_perms=1000 takes 8 s, and the whole downstream script 1.8 min. The substantive cost was that without cell 54 the inflow branch had no source→target significance at all — it could not report a single directed interaction, which is the one thing this branch exists to provide. run_inflow_downstream.py now performs all five steps and every figure the tutorial draws (80 figures, 0 blank).

Results, and how far they can be pushed

The method's own top LRs by the conditional maximum are CNTN2^CNTN2, NCAM1^NCAM1, C3^C3AR1, PECAM1^PECAM1, JAM3^JAM3, CD99^CD99 — five homotypic adhesion pairs plus complement. As whole LRs the two requested pairs are mid-table: GRN^SORT1 54th and ANXA1^FPR1 72nd of 633, identically in the conditional and unconditional rankings.

The informative result is not the LR rank but the directed cell-type pair, which is what ALARMIST motif 1 actually claims:

ALARMIST motif-1 armlr_meanpRank within that LR (of 81 source→target pairs)
ANXA1→FPR1, MES-like → mGAM0.12630.000999 (permutation floor)2 / 81
GRN→SORT1, mGAM → MES-like0.02021.020 / 81

Inflow corroborates one arm of the loop and not the other. The MES-like → mGAM arm is the second-strongest of all 81 directed pairs for ANXA1^FPR1 and sits at the permutation floor; the mGAM → MES-like arm returns p = 1.0, which is the weakest possible outcome of a one-sided specificity test, not a marginal result.

The caveat that limits how far this can be pushed: the rankings are dominated by self-self pairs. GRN^SORT1's top four directed pairs are Vascular→Vascular (0.283), mGAM→mGAM (0.261), Glial-Neuronal→Glial-Neuronal (0.213) and non-mGAM→non-mGAM (0.161); ANXA1^FPR1's top is mGAM→mGAM (0.208), above the MES-like→mGAM arm. This is a direct consequence of the formula: a neighbourhood-averaged ligand term multiplied by the receiver's own receptor expression scores highly whenever a cell type both expresses the ligand and clusters with itself. Read the off-diagonal cells; treat the diagonal as a co-localisation baseline, not a result — which is exactly what pair_proximity is for.

Finally, the statistical caveat that must travel with every p-value from this branch. compute_global_specificity permutes labels across cells. Its p-values are therefore cell-level at n = 100,190, and are pseudoreplicated by roughly four orders of magnitude relative to the 13 TMA cores that are the actual experimental units. This applies to the grade contrast too: it is a per-group specificity test, not a high-vs-low contrast — region_global_interactions.csv has no contrast column, no effect size and no direction. When the same question is asked at the correct replicate unit (7 high vs 6 low punches, Mann-Whitney, BH-corrected), nothing survives correction, though that design has a hard p-floor of 0.001166 and is underpowered, so the null is weak evidence of absence rather than evidence of no effect. Treat the direction of an effect from this branch as the result, never the magnitude of the p.

title: Factorisation, the default tier, and the second local metric
html:
NMF on the LIANA+ output

Script: scripts/comparators/liana/run_nmf.py. Source of the recipe: the NMF section of bivariate.ipynb (markdown cells 47–49, code cells 50–55). Four runs exist on disk: nmf_bivariate, nmf_inflow, nmf_bivariate_default, nmf_inflow_default.

What the factorisation returns, and why it is the one output shaped like ALARMIST

li.multi.nmf is a thin wrapper around sklearn.decomposition.NMF plus a rank chooser. It factorises the local score matrix lrdata.X (locations × features) into two non-negative matrices:

  • W — obsm['NMF_W'], locations × factors. Entry (i,k) is how strongly factor k is used at cell i. Retrieved as a tidy frame by li.ut.get_factor_scores(obsm_key='NMF_W').
  • H — varm['NMF_H'], features × factors. Entry (j,k) is how much feature j defines factor k. Retrieved by li.ut.get_variable_loadings(varm_key='NMF_H').

A "feature" means different things on the two inputs, and this is the entire point of running both: on bivariate a feature is an LR pair (GRN^SORT1); on inflow it is a sender cell type × LR pair (mGAM^GRN^SORT1), because inflow puts the sender identity into the score itself.

This is the only comparator output in the whole benchmark that shares ALARMIST's shape — ALARMIST's BPTF returns a patches × motifs loading matrix and an LRI × motifs factor matrix, which is W and H with a coarser location unit. Every other method here returns a ranked list of interactions, a per-edge score, or a per-target importance, none of which can be laid next to a motif. That is why the NMF branch exists at all; it is not the authors' headline analysis.

The calls, as run

Input assembly differs by branch, because the two upstream runs persist differently. Nothing is recomputed here — run_nmf.py reads what the upstream scripts wrote:

# bivariate branch: rebuild an AnnData from the persisted local score matrix
z = np.load(f"{in_dir}/data/local_scores.npz", allow_pickle=True)
lrdata = ad.AnnData(X=np.asarray(z["values"], dtype=np.float32),
                    obs=pd.DataFrame(index=z["cells"].astype(str)),
                    var=pd.DataFrame(index=z["pairs"].astype(str)))

# inflow branch: the AnnData was already written out
lrdata = sc.read_h5ad(f"{in_dir}/data/inflow_lrdata.h5ad")

Then, identically for both:

li.multi.nmf(lrdata,
             n_components=None,       # tutorial: n_components=None  (elbow-selected) -- same
             k_range=range(1, 21),    # tutorial: argument OMITTED -> package default range(1, 11)
             inplace=True,            # tutorial: inplace=True
             random_state=0,          # tutorial: random_state=0
             max_iter=200,            # tutorial: max_iter=200
             verbose=True)            # tutorial: verbose=True

loadings = li.ut.get_variable_loadings(lrdata, varm_key='NMF_H').set_index('index')
scores   = li.ut.get_factor_scores(lrdata, obsm_key='NMF_W')

Command lines actually issued (the cellchatdb2 pair; the default pair is the same with --in-dir pointing at default / default_inflow):

python run_nmf.py --input bivariate --k-max 21 \
    --in-dir  results/comparators/liana/GBM/cellchatdb2 \
    --out-dir results/comparators/liana/GBM/nmf_bivariate

python run_nmf.py --input inflow --k-max 21 \
    --in-dir  results/comparators/liana/GBM/cellchatdb2_inflow \
    --out-dir results/comparators/liana/GBM/nmf_inflow

Two things the runner adds that the tutorial has no counterpart for, both mechanical: it hard-stops if the input contains a negative value (NMF is undefined there — and it does not clip, because clipping would hide the problem; see the Moran's-R section, where this stop is what would fire), and it redraws the elbow figure itself. The redraw is necessary because li.multi.nmf calls _plot_elbow internally, which draws with plotnine, not matplotlib — plt.gcf() is an empty canvas afterwards, so saving the "current figure" writes a blank PNG. That same plotnine return-type trap produced four all-white PNGs elsewhere in this comparator before it was caught.

Deviation: a cross-punch reproducibility filter applied before the factorisation

The tutorial factorises whatever li.mt.bivariate returned. We insert one filter first.

Rule. The LIANA+ paper retains interactions present in at least 10 of its 28 tissue sections. This TMA has 13 punches (obs['tma_id'], ids 1–6 and 8–14; 7 high-grade, 6 low-grade). Scaled proportionally, 10/28 → ≥5 of 13. A feature counts as present in a punch if it is non-zero in at least one cell of that punch:

present[i] = (X[cores == c] > 0).any(axis=0)      # per punch c
keep       = present.sum(axis=0) >= 5              # --min-punches 5, the default

Why. The whole slide is a mosaic of 13 physically separate cores. Without the filter a feature that is non-zero in a single core — a fragment of necrosis, one vessel-rich punch — enters the factorisation on equal footing with one that recurs across the cohort, and NMF is perfectly happy to spend a factor on it. The filter forces the recovered programs to be built out of interactions that reproduce across punches. Per-feature counts are written to data/punch_presence.csv so the cut can be audited without re-running.

Measured effect, and it is very asymmetric:

BranchFeatures beforeAfter ≥5/13% keptMedian punches per feature
nmf_bivariate131131100%12 / 13
nmf_inflow4,6082,70458.7%6 / 13
nmf_bivariate_default388388100%12 / 13
nmf_inflow_default9,4486,17865.4%7 / 13

On bivariate the filter is a no-op — not because it was designed to be, but because a bivariate feature is a whole LR pair pooled over every cell type, and the median such pair is already detectable in 12 of 13 punches. On inflow, where a feature is one sender's use of one LR pair, the median is 6 of 13 and the filter removes 41.3% of the feature space. So the filter is load-bearing on exactly one of the two branches, and any comparison of the two decompositions is comparing 131 pair-level features against 2,704 sender-resolved ones.

Deviation: k_range = range(1, 21) instead of the default range(1, 11)

li.multi.nmf's signature is k_range: range = range(1, 11) and the tutorial does not override it. We pass range(1, 21).

Why, mechanically. Rank selection is kneed.KneeLocator (Kneedle) on the error-vs-k curve, with direction='decreasing', curve='convex', interp_method='interp1d', S=1. Kneedle min-max normalises both axes over the window it is handed before looking for the point of maximum curvature. Change the window and you change the normalisation, hence the knee. Ranks obtained on different windows are therefore not comparable numbers — not approximately comparable, not comparable at all. Measured on this data:

k_rangebivariate rankinflow rankStatus
range(1,11) — the package default3—inflow's elbow lies outside the window
range(1,41)311historical; not comparable to the row below
range(1,21) — in force67both branches on the same window, neither rank at a boundary

The default window is too narrow to contain the inflow branch's knee at all, which is the concrete reason it was widened. It was widened to 20 rather than 40 because a knee at the top of the window is a truncation rather than a detection — run_nmf.py warns explicitly when a rank lands on either endpoint, and neither of these does. Cost is not the constraint: a single NMF fit takes 18.7 s at k=5 and gets faster with k (10.8 s at k=40); the whole cellchatdb2 NMF runs are 0.9 wall-min each.

Provenance: NMF on inflow output is our composition, not an author-demonstrated path

This has to be stated before any result from this branch is read.

  • inflow_score.ipynb contains no NMF section. li.multi.nmf appears only in bivariate.ipynb. Applying it to inflow output is our own construction.
  • The authors' own answer for unsupervised decomposition at single-cell resolution is a different factorisation. The LIANA+ decision tree routes Spatially-resolved → Single-cell → Unsupervised to Communication Programs = Inflow + MOFA-Flex (inflow_mofaflex.ipynb), not to NMF. That branch has since been run separately.
  • Conversely, li.mt.bivariate sits under the tree's spot-based branch, so NMF-on-bivariate is the tutorial-sanctioned composition run on data of the wrong resolution.

Neither combination is the authors' prescribed route for this data, and we ran both deliberately rather than picking one: bivariate is the composition the authors actually demonstrate, inflow is the input appropriate to the resolution. Running both turns an awkward choice into a measurement — how much of the recovered program structure is set by the upstream feature construction rather than by the tissue?

What the two decompositions actually recover — and they disagree

Spatial Pearson correlation between the two NMF_W matrices over the 100,190 shared cells (full matrix: results/comparators/liana/GBM/nmf_factor_correlation.csv):

bivariate factorbest-matching inflow factorr
F1inflow F7+0.230
F2inflow F1−0.041
F3inflow F3+0.378
F4inflow F3+0.232
F5inflow F3+0.225
F6inflow F7+0.430

Best match anywhere is r = 0.43; five of seven inflow factors have max |r| < 0.3 against any bivariate factor; three separate bivariate factors map onto the same inflow F3. The two decompositions are not nested — bivariate is not a coarse summary of inflow, it is a different partition of the same tissue.

The organising axis differs qualitatively, which is the clearer statement:

BranchTop features per factor
bivariate — organised by LR family F1 JAG1^NOTCH1/2 · F2 immune/complement (C3^C3AR1, GAS6^AXL/MERTK) · F3 ECM (COL4A1/A2^CD44, LAMC1^CD44) · F4 TNC^SDC4, APP^SORL1 · F5 neurexin (NRXN2^CLSTN1/ADGRL1/NLGN3) · F6 DLL3/DLL1^NOTCH1/2
inflow — organised by sender cell type F1 Glial-Neuronal · F2 OPC-like · F3 MES-like · F4 NPC-like · F5 AC-like · F6 Glial-Neuronal · F7 NPC-like

Every one of inflow's seven factors is anchored to a single sender; not one bivariate factor is. Inflow splits the NOTCH ligands by who is sending them — OPC-like^DLL3^NOTCH1/2 in F2 versus NPC-like^DLL3^NOTCH1/2 in F7 — where bivariate collapses all DLL3/DLL1→NOTCH signalling into a single F6 regardless of sender. That is a resolution gain attributable to the finer feature space, not a relabelling.

Carry this forward: a reviewer shown only the bivariate NMF would report that this TMA contains six communication programs organised by ligand family; shown only the inflow NMF, seven organised by sender cell type. Both are legitimate runs of the same package on the same slide. Any claim about "communication programs" from this class of method is unreadable without the upstream configuration attached.

The rank is the least robust number this comparator produces

li.multi.nmf selects the elbow on mean absolute error (_calculate_error in liana/multi/_nmf.py). An L1 criterion on a matrix that is 83.62% zeros (bivariate) or 99.45% zeros (inflow) has a formidable trivial competitor: predicting zero everywhere. Recomputed directly from the stored W, H and the matching input columns:

RunRankRel. Frobenius errorFraction of SS capturedAchieved MAEZero-predictor MAEBeats zero?
nmf_bivariate60.760742%0.0805830.072522no
nmf_inflow70.777140%0.0152870.011817no
nmf_bivariate_default60.758242.5%0.0852560.077797no
nmf_inflow_default50.829431.2%0.0166170.012344no

None of the four fits beats the all-zero predictor on the metric its own rank was chosen with. This is a property of L1 on an extremely sparse non-negative matrix rather than a defect in the run — the Frobenius fit is respectable (30–43% of sum-of-squares) and the factors are spatially coherent. But it means the elbow is a feature of the loss surface, not a count of programs the tissue has. Rank 6 / rank 7 must always be reported with the relative Frobenius error and the zero-predictor baseline beside them. run_nmf.py now computes all four numbers itself, writes them into the manifest (rel_frobenius_error, frac_sumsq_captured, mae, mae_zero_predictor, beats_zero_predictor) and prints an explicit warning when the fit loses to zero — so the caveat cannot be dropped by accident.

Ranked by how much they move the answer, the three upstream choices are:

Upstream choiceMeasured effect on the rankClean?
bandwidth 18.75 → 13.1454 µm (k_range 1..40 both)inflow 11 → 7yes — only bandwidth differs
elbow window 1..10 / 1..40 / 1..20 (bivariate)3 / 3 / 6yes — only the window differs
LR database, CellChatDB v2 → consensus (k_range 1..20 both)bivariate 6 → 6; inflow 7 → 5yes — refit on the matched window

Bandwidth and the elbow window move it hard; the database moves it least. Note that the bandwidth of 13.1454 µm is itself derived from ALARMIST's 50 µm patch edge by equal-area correspondence — an open deviation from our own benchmark contract, which forbids matching a method's spatial scale to ALARMIST's. So "LIANA finds 7 programs" is partly a function of a number imported from the method it is being compared against. That is a judgement call, still contested, and it is recorded as unresolved rather than settled.

The default tier — LIANA's own LR resource

What it is, and the fact that it was late

Our benchmark contract (.claude/skills/comparator-benchmark/SKILL.md, lines 51–54) requires two tiers per method, in this order: default — the method's own LR database, which proves the method was used as its authors recommend — then cellchatdb2, which removes the LR database as a confounder against ALARMIST.

For a long time only cellchatdb2 existed. The default tier was added afterwards, by scripts/comparators/liana/run_default_tier.sh, and the runs table recorded it as "still not run" until then. Stating this plainly because the contract specifies an order and we did not follow it.

The driver is five steps, --db consensus, every other argument identical to the cellchatdb2 tier:

run_liana.py            --h5ad data/xenium_mm_final_cell_id.h5ad --db consensus --out-dir $R/default
run_inflow.py           --h5ad data/xenium_mm_final_cell_id.h5ad --db consensus --out-dir $R/default_inflow
run_inflow_downstream.py --in-dir $R/default_inflow --h5ad ... --db consensus
run_nmf.py --k-max 21 --input bivariate --in-dir $R/default        --out-dir $R/nmf_bivariate_default
run_nmf.py --k-max 21 --input inflow    --in-dir $R/default_inflow --out-dir $R/nmf_inflow_default

The two resources are a real comparison, not a formality. LIANA's consensus has 4,624 unique (ligand, receptor) pairs against CellChatDB v2's 3,218, and they share only 1,663 — 36.0% of consensus, 51.7% of CellChatDB. Both required LRs (GRN^SORT1, ANXA1^FPR1) are in both.

The key result: the LR database is not a confounder for any per-interaction statistic

Both tiers were joined on their shared entries and compared value by value:

ComparisonShared entriesmax |difference|
bivariate global Moran's R79 pairs0.000e+00 (means also identical: 0.02256821 both)
bivariate morans_pvals, mean, std79 pairs0.0 each
inflow lr_mean, source × target × LR23,787 rows0.0
inflow pval, source × target × LR23,787 rows0 rows differ

Why this is structural rather than lucky. LIANA scores each LR pair independently: the local metric is computed from that pair's own two genes and the spatial weights, the global Moran's R from that pair's own local scores, and the permutation p-value from shuffling labels for that pair. There is no cross-pair normalisation anywhere in bivariate or inflow — no rank transform across pairs, no library-size term that depends on how many pairs are in the resource, no shared variance-stabilisation. Adding 3,000 more pairs to the resource therefore cannot move the score of a pair that was already there.

Swapping the resource changes exactly three things:

  1. which pairs are tested — 388 vs 131 bivariate, 9,448 vs 4,608 inflow features;
  2. the ranking and multiple-testing denominator — GRN^SORT1 moves from rank 33/131 to 77/388 with an unchanged Moran's R of 0.035702; ANXA1^FPR1 from 60/131 to 187/388, R unchanged at 0.013804;
  3. the feature space the factorisation sees.

Consequence for anything quoted from this method: a LIANA rank is a statement about the resource; a LIANA score is not. Report ranks with the resource named, or report the score.

A confound we created ourselves, published internally, and then caught

This is recorded as a cautionary tale, not as a result.

What happened. The first version of run_default_tier.sh called run_nmf.py without --k-max. run_nmf.py:31 defaults it to 11. So the default tier's two NMFs were fitted with "k_range": [1, 11, 1] while the cellchatdb2 pair carried [1, 21, 1]. They gave rank 4 and rank 4, against 6 and 7.

The wrong headline it produced. "The LR database moves the factor count from 6/7 to 4/4" — plausible, quotable, and wrong. It was a database × window effect, attributable to neither, and it walked straight into a trap this repository had already documented in its own Choosing k_range section: Kneedle normalises over the window it is given. The claim survived one full round of documentation before being caught by reading the manifests rather than the prose.

Resolution. Both default-tier NMFs were refitted with --k-max 21, and run_default_tier.sh now passes it explicitly with a comment at both call sites saying it must never be omitted. On the matched window:

Branchcellchatdb2defaultFeatures
bivariaterank 6rank 6131 → 388
inflowrank 7rank 52,704 → 6,178 (post-filter)

So the database's effect on the factor count is the weakest of the three upstream choices: zero for bivariate — rank 6 either way, despite the feature count tripling — and 7 → 5 for inflow, against bandwidth's 11 → 7 and the elbow window's 3 → 6. What survives is that the resource changes which features are factorised, not how many programs the elbow finds.

The lesson worth keeping: the confound was created by omitting a single argument, and any cross-tier rank comparison must assert that the windows are equal before comparing.

The default tier exists to answer whether the resource confounds the statistics; the persisted score/loading tables answer that, and the figures would duplicate the cellchatdb2 tree's layout on a different feature set. It is a contract shortfall, not a loss — the underlying data is on disk.

The second local metric — cosine vs morans

The call, and what is held fixed

li.mt.bivariate.show_functions() lists eight local metrics; only cosine — the tutorial's value — had been run. results/comparators/liana/GBM/cellchatdb2_morans/ adds a second arm in which local_name is the only thing that changes: same resource (CellChatDB v2, 3,218 pairs), same nz_prop=0.02, same 131 pairs tested, same bandwidth 13.1454 µm / cutoff 0.1 / set_diag=True, same 100 permutations, same seed, same 100,197 cells, same whole-slide run. 3.6 wall-min, 35 figures.

li.mt.bivariate(adata,
                resource=cellchatdb_v2,   # ['ligand','receptor'] frame, handed over directly
                local_name='morans',      # tutorial / our first arm: 'cosine'
                global_name='morans',     # unchanged -- it was ALREADY 'morans'
                n_perms=100,
                mask_negatives=False,
                add_categories=True,
                nz_prop=0.02,
                use_raw=False)

morans here is the local bivariate Moran's R; LIANA's own function table cites the SpatialDM paper for it. Because global_name was already morans, the two arms share their global statistic by construction — which is what makes this a clean isolation of the local metric.

What changed, and what did not

The global statistic is bit-identical. Global Moran's R, its p-values and the entire 131-pair ranking match across the two runs to max |Δ| = 0.0. global_scores.csv is byte-for-byte the same file. Only lrdata.X differs.

The local scores are almost unrelated. Per-pair Pearson correlation between the two local matrices, over all 100,197 cells:

r
median over the 131 pairs0.195
range0.095 – 0.337
GRN^SORT10.189
ANXA1^FPR10.253

They are not even the same kind of object:

cosinemorans
range over 100,197 × 131[0, 1.0000002][−14.084, 73.273]
zeros83.6214%0.0000%
negatives04,378,791 (33.4%)

Two consequences, both load-bearing.

  1. "Is this interaction spatially structured overall" is robust to the metric; "which cells carry it" is almost entirely determined by it. Any figure, niche assignment, or factorisation built on the local scores is a statement about the chosen metric as much as about the tissue. At a median r of 0.195, the two metrics do not agree about where an interaction happens.
  2. Moran's R is not NMF-admissible. 33.4% of its entries are negative and none are zero, so li.multi.nmf could not have been run on it at all — run_nmf.py's hard stop would fire. This retroactively justifies cosine as the NMF input. It is a post-hoc justification, not the original reason (cosine was chosen because it is the tutorial's value), and it is recorded as such.

It also exposes a latent assumption in the cross-punch filter. That filter defines presence as "non-zero in at least one cell", and run_nmf.py implements it as X > 0. For cosine (no negatives) X > 0 and X != 0 coincide; for morans they do not, and a third of the matrix would be silently counted as absent. The filter is only correct for a non-negative local metric — it happened to be applied to one.

The cross-method use: LIANA's Moran's R against SpatialDM's

The reason for running this arm is not internal. With global_name='morans' LIANA computes the same statistic as the SpatialDM comparator, so the two methods become directly comparable on a shared quantity rather than on rank overlap. All 131 LIANA pairs appear in SpatialDM's union of 1,662 interactions across the 13 cores, so no key repair is needed. Taking LIANA's whole-slide Moran's R against SpatialDM's median per-core z:

The caveat is not optional. This is agreement between two implementations each at its own default spatial scale — SpatialDM run per core at roughly 709 neighbours per cell, LIANA run whole-slide at a 28.2 µm support with a median of 14 neighbours — because SKILL.md:45-46 forbids harmonising spatial scale across methods. The residual disagreement therefore mixes implementation and spatial scale and cannot be attributed to either. The honest reading of the headline is "Spearman 0.62 across a ~50× difference in neighbourhood size", not "the two implementations agree to r = 0.62".

title: MOFA-Flex, factor annotation, LRIC/cross-PCF, LR-MISTy, the punch-level test, and the defects we found
html:
MOFA-Flex on inflow — the route the authors actually prescribe

LIANA+'s README ships a decision tree. Its Spatially-resolved → Single-cell → Unsupervised leaf reads "Communication Programs — Inflow + MOFA-Flex", demonstrated in inflow_mofaflex.ipynb. Our earlier NMF work (li.multi.nmf on inflow output) is our own composition — inflow_score.ipynb contains no NMF section, and NMF appears only in bivariate.ipynb. Until 2026-08-04 DEVIATIONS.md called MOFA-Flex "the untested, author-sanctioned alternative". This section is the run that closed that gap. The result is the single most reportable thing in the whole LIANA+ pass, and it is a finding about the comparator, not about the tissue.

Report this honestly rather than quoting the significant hits.

An NMF factor over LR-pair features is not a gene expression profile, and generate_lr_geneset only transfers a gene-level weight onto the ligand and the receptor of a pair. What the test actually asks is "do the LR pairs this factor loads on happen to involve genes that are PROGENy targets of pathway P" — a much weaker statement than pathway activity, and one that a single dominant adhesion pair can dominate. The caveat is written into the script's own docstring, before the first result was produced.
